meta.title: R3 research studio: which system, which boundary, which method? Briefs, method families, scales and exemplars
meta.note: The three briefs, Prairie Campus, Prairie City, the Plains Grid and the exemplars are illustrative. The fit notes are judgments for teaching, not rules: several families can answer one question.

families.label: Optimization
families.answers: What is the best choice under stated rules and goals?
families.needs: Decisions, a goal, rules (constraints) and their data.
families.tools: Solvers for linear programs (LP) and mixed-integer programs (MILP), such as HiGHS, with Pyomo, JuMP or PyPSA
families.limit: Best only inside the model, for its goal. A deterministic run may treat future weather and demand as known ([[perfect-foresight|perfect foresight]]) unless built otherwise (a rolling horizon): say what each decision can know.

families.label: Simulation
families.answers: What happens when the system runs by given rules, under given conditions?
families.needs: Operating rules, inputs over time and the designs to test.
families.tools: Production-cost and power-flow simulators, or your own code
families.limit: It tests the designs you give it; it does not search for the best one.

families.label: Statistics and econometrics
families.answers: How much, how often, and did a change cause an effect?
families.needs: Observed data with variation; for a causal claim, a comparison group.
families.limit: It sees only the observed past; causal claims rest on assumptions about the comparison.

families.label: Machine learning
families.answers: What will the next value be, or which pattern is this?
families.needs: Many examples, honest baselines and data held back for testing.
families.limit: Least reliable outside the range of its training data, and it explains little about why.

families.label: System dynamics
families.answers: How do stocks, flows and feedback shape a trend over years?
families.needs: A causal-loop structure and parameters for each flow.
families.limit: It works with aggregates, and many parameters rest on judgment.

families.label: Agent-based modeling
families.answers: How do many deciding actors produce a system outcome?
families.needs: Rules for each kind of actor, and data on how they behave.
families.limit: Results depend on behavior rules that are hard to check against data.

families.label: Equilibrium modeling
families.answers: Where do prices and quantities settle when many markets or players interact?
families.needs: Supply and demand, market rules and how players respond to prices.
families.tools: Complementarity models in Pyomo or GAMS
families.limit: Static versions describe a settled state, not the path to it; most simplify how players behave.

families.label: Qualitative methods
families.answers: How and why do people and institutions decide as they do?
families.needs: Interviews, documents or cases, with consent and a plan for the analysis.
families.tools: Interview guides, document analysis, coding of transcripts
families.limit: It gives no numbers that generalize; this course teaches it at awareness level only.

families.label: Mixed methods
families.answers: Questions that need both numbers and people's reasons.
families.needs: A model or data analysis, a qualitative part, and a plan for how each informs the other.
families.limit: More time, and both parts must answer the same question.

scales.name: Device and plant
scales.decides: what to install at one site, and how to run it
scales.who: the owner, within tariffs and codes
scales.horizon: a day to the equipment's life

scales.name: Microgrid and community
scales.who: a facility owner or co-op, under the utility's rules

scales.name: Regional grid
scales.decides: commitment, dispatch, reserves, transmission, new plants
scales.who: the grid operator or utility, and regulators
scales.horizon: the next hour to several decades

scales.name: City and region
scales.decides: buildings, heat, transport, land use, local supply
scales.who: city and county, utilities and owners

scales.name: Nation
scales.decides: targets, policy instruments, infrastructure, security stocks, trade

bins.label: Decided or computed
bins.sub: in the study: it decides or computes these

bins.label: Fixed inputs
bins.sub: in the study: used, but not changed by it

bins.label: Left out
bins.sub: outside the study: stated as a limit

briefs.question: What sizes of solar, battery and backup generator keep Prairie Campus's hospital supplied through a three-day winter outage at the lowest 20-year cost, compared with today's diesel generator alone?
briefs.scaleWhy: S1: one campus that can run on its own, sized by its owner under the utility's rules. The tariff and the feeder's limits come from the regional grid above.
briefs.assume: Assumed: the switch to running alone ([[islanding|islanding]]) works. The study checks whether there is enough energy, not the switch itself.

boundary.text: Sizes of solar, battery and generator
boundary.why: These are the decisions the study makes.

boundary.text: The hospital's critical load, hour by hour
boundary.why: A measured or estimated input; the study does not change it.

boundary.text: The utility's tariff and the feeder's export limit
boundary.why: Set at the scale above; fixed inputs here.

boundary.text: Hourly winter weather for solar output
boundary.why: An input: a design winter, or several past ones.

boundary.text: Diesel fuel stored on site when the outage starts
boundary.why: A fixed limit in the outage case.

boundary.text: Wholesale prices across the Plains Grid
boundary.why: The campus pays a tariff, not wholesale prices: say so as a limit.

boundary.text: Road access for fuel trucks during the storm
boundary.why: Left out and stated: the design must last three days on stored fuel.

boundary.text: Who owns the system and who pays for it
boundary.why: A separate question about ownership, noted as a limit of the cost result.

steps.label: 1 second
steps.why: Seconds matter for switching, protection and stability: a separate study, which this one assumes succeeds.

steps.label: 5 minutes
steps.why: Useful for checking short-term operating schedules; switching and stability need a separate, faster study.

steps.label: 1 hour
steps.why: Hourly steps follow solar's daily cycle and the battery's charge.

steps.label: 1 day
steps.why: A daily step hides the night, when the battery must carry the load.

steps.label: 1 year
steps.why: A yearly total cannot show whether the lights stay on in hour 40.

horizons.label: One day
horizons.why: Shorter than the three-day outage itself.

horizons.label: The outage days only
horizons.why: Enough to test survival, not to price 20 years of ownership.

horizons.label: A typical year plus the outage
horizons.why: A normal year for running costs, the outage case for survival; building costs spread over 20 years.

horizons.label: 20 years, hour by hour
horizons.why: Complete, but much larger than needed if the years repeat.

opt: A sizing model (a [[linear-program|linear]] or [[mixed-integer-program|mixed-integer]] program) finds the cheapest mix that keeps the critical load served.
sim: Simulate candidate designs hour by hour through the outage; it compares the designs you supply.
stat: Past outage records can set the outage cases, but cannot choose the sizes.
ml: Nothing here needs a pattern learned from many examples.
sd: Feedback over years does not drive a three-day outage.
abm: One owner decides: there are no interacting actors to model.
eq: No market settles here: the campus pays a fixed tariff.
qual: Interviews with hospital staff can set which loads are critical.
mixed: A sizing model plus interviews that define the critical load.

defence.choice: A sizing [[mixed-integer-program|mixed-integer program]] (MILP) that picks the cheapest sizes keeping the critical load served.
defence.resolution: Hourly steps over a typical year, plus a three-day winter outage.
defence.alt1: The generator has a minimum load and comes in whole units, which only whole-number decisions capture.
defence.alt2: The question asks for the cheapest mix, not a ranking of mixes I already have; a simulation still checks the chosen design.
defence.limit: [[perfect-foresight|Perfect foresight]] during the outage: the model knows the coming weather.
defence.check: Test the chosen design in a rule-based simulation that does not know the future.

briefs.short: Did the rebate reach low-income homes?
briefs.question: Did Prairie City's 2023 heat-pump rebate raise installations in its low-income neighborhoods, compared with similar neighborhoods in cities without a rebate?
briefs.scaleWhy: S3: a city program, set by the council with local money and rules. Federal incentives come from the nation above; the homes below act on them.

boundary.text: Heat-pump installations per 1,000 homes, by neighborhood and month
boundary.why: The outcome the study measures.

boundary.text: The choice of comparison neighborhoods
boundary.why: A design decision of the study, and the one that matters most.

boundary.text: The rebate's rules, amount and start date
boundary.why: Fixed facts of the program.

boundary.text: Neighborhood income and housing data from the census
boundary.why: Input data, used to match similar neighborhoods.

boundary.text: Federal tax credits available everywhere
boundary.why: Assumed to affect both groups alike; check eligibility and other policies that could shift their trends differently.

boundary.text: Whether the heat pumps lowered bills
boundary.why: A different question, for a later study.

boundary.text: Installers' waiting lists
boundary.why: Left out and stated: they may have limited uptake.

boundary.text: Grid upgrades for the new heating load
boundary.why: Outside a question about uptake.

steps.label: 1 hour
steps.why: Installations are not counted by the hour.

steps.label: 1 day
steps.why: Daily counts are noisy and mostly zero; months say as much.

steps.label: 1 month
steps.why: Monthly counts show the change around the rebate's start.

steps.label: 1 year
steps.why: Only a few points before and after 2023.

horizons.label: 2023 to 2025, after the start
horizons.why: No years before the rebate to compare with.

horizons.label: 2019 to 2025, before and after
horizons.why: Several years on each side of the start, to compare trends.

horizons.label: To 2050
horizons.why: A projection to 2050 answers a different, predictive question.

opt: Nothing to choose: the rebate has already happened.
sim: A simulation would assume how households behave; here the records show what happened.
stat: [[difference-in-differences|Difference-in-differences]]: compare the change before and after with similar neighborhoods that had no rebate.
ml: It can help pick similar neighborhoods, but predicting installations is not the question.
sd: Years of feedback are not the question; one program's effect is.
abm: It could explore how adoption spreads between neighbors, but it assumes the behavior this study must measure.
eq: No market price settles this question.
qual: Interviews with installers and landlords can explain why uptake differed.
mixed: The comparison says how much; interviews say why.

defence.same: a before-and-after count in Prairie City alone
defence.choice: A [[difference-in-differences|difference-in-differences]] comparison of installations in low-income neighborhoods.
defence.alt1: Prices and federal credits changed everywhere at once, so a before-and-after count mixes them with the rebate.
defence.alt2: It would assume how households respond, which is what this study must measure.
defence.limit: It assumes both groups would have moved in parallel without the rebate.
defence.check: Compare their trends before 2023, and repeat with a second comparison group.

briefs.short: A large load that can pause
briefs.question: How would a 300 MW load that can pause for up to four hours during scarcity change the Plains Grid's [[expected-unserved-energy|expected unserved energy]] in a heat-wave year, compared with the same load running flat?
briefs.scaleWhy: S2: [[resource-adequacy|adequacy]] is planned for a region, such as a market operator's or a utility's planning area, with its transfer limits and assumptions about its neighbors. The load only decides when it pauses.
briefs.assume: Pausing rule (illustrative): up to four hours in a row per event, at most ten events a year, and paused work is not made up later. Paused energy is counted apart from unserved energy.

boundary.text: When the load pauses, hour by hour
boundary.why: Set inside the study by a pausing rule.

boundary.text: Random generator outages
boundary.why: Drawn many times by the study, to give a range.

boundary.text: Hourly demand and weather for a heat-wave year
boundary.why: Input data: a past heat-wave year, or a scaled one.

boundary.text: Today's plants and the transfer limits between zones
boundary.why: Fixed: the question asks about the system as it is.

boundary.text: Imports from neighboring grids
boundary.why: Fixed limits, stated.

boundary.text: The load's contract: who pays for pausing
boundary.why: A separate question about contracts and tariffs.

boundary.text: Voltage and stability in the seconds after a trip
boundary.why: A different time scale, and a different study.

boundary.text: New plants built because the load arrived
boundary.why: A planning question; this one keeps the fleet fixed.

steps.label: 5 minutes
steps.why: Finer than adequacy studies usually need.

steps.label: 1 hour
steps.why: Adequacy studies count unserved energy hour by hour.

steps.label: 1 day
steps.why: A daily step hides the evening peak.

horizons.label: The hottest day
horizons.why: One day misses the other tight hours of the year.

horizons.label: The heat-wave week
horizons.why: Catches the worst week, not the rest of the year.

horizons.label: One year, run many times
horizons.why: A full year, repeated with random outages, gives the expected value and its range.

horizons.label: 20 to 30 years
horizons.why: A planning horizon, for a question that keeps the fleet fixed.

opt: A dispatch model can choose the best hours to pause inside each simulated year.
sim: Run the year many times with random outages ([[monte-carlo|Monte Carlo]]) and count unserved energy with and without pausing.
stat: Past outage rates set the random draws.
ml: The load is new: there are no examples to learn from.
sd: Feedback over years is not the question.
abm: If several large loads competed to pause, their interaction could matter; with one load it does not.
eq: Prices are not the metric here.
qual: Talking to the operator can set realistic pausing rules.
mixed: A simulation, with operator interviews to set the pausing rules.

defence.same: a check of the single worst hour
defence.choice: A [[monte-carlo|Monte Carlo]] adequacy simulation that runs the heat-wave year many times with random outages.
defence.resolution: Hourly steps; one year, run many times.
defence.alt1: The question asks how often and how much, not only whether.
defence.alt2: One deterministic dispatch run cannot estimate the expected shortfall across random outages; repeated outage cases are needed, possibly with optimized dispatch inside each.
defence.limit: Outages are drawn independently, while a heat wave can cause several at once.
defence.check: Add a run with linked outages as a sensitivity.

rubric.title: Rate your design against the rubric
rubric.lede: The course rubric's own words. R3 builds two competences of nine.

competences.look: the scale and the three boundary lists are stated; the rest of Framing (audience, metric with units, counterfactual, falsification) comes from your R1 card.
two alternatives named, one from another family, each rejected for a reason tied to the question.

rubric.note: Your rating stays in this browser. A studio is practice, not a certificate: the course's readiness claim also needs the checkpoints and a research capstone.

exemplars.title: Two method defenses for the same question
exemplars.task: Defend a method for: “How sensitive is a national storage build-out to a one-year disruption of one mineral, and which design choices reduce the risk?”

parts.note: A family is named, but nothing says why it fits a question about sensitivity and risk.

parts.text: it is the standard tool for national planning
parts.note: Chosen by habit: the rubric's Developing anchor for method fit.
Optimal only inside the model's assumptions, and one run gives no range.
A scale, but no boundary, time step or horizon.

answers.label: Strong answer

parts.text: a conditional planning study: how do model-optimal storage plans change across disruption cases?
parts.note: Says what an optimization can answer here: the best plan under each case, not a forecast of what will be built.

parts.text: the national power system's builds and hourly operation; mineral supply enters as given disruption cases; recycling left out
parts.note: The three boundary lists: what is decided or computed, what is fixed and what is left out.

parts.text: run under many disruption cases drawn at random
parts.note: Matches the question: “how sensitive” needs a range, not one plan.

parts.text: yearly steps to 2040, [[representative-period|representative hours]] inside each year
parts.note: Time step and horizon stated, matched to a build-out over years.

parts.text: a single run with expected prices
parts.note: A simpler version of the same family, rejected for a reason.

parts:
; it hides the risk the question asks about
Alternative 2:

parts.text: a system-dynamics model of mineral supply
parts.note: Another family, rejected for a reason: what the Proficient anchor asks for.

parts:
; it captures market feedback, not the grid's hourly needs
Main limit:

parts.text: perfect foresight inside each case; the results are model-optimal plans, not predicted deployment
parts.note: The limit stated, with what the results do and do not mean.

parts.text: fixing early builds before the disruption is known
parts.note: The limit partly mitigated: the Strong anchor for method fit.

diff.label: Why this family
diff.good: Tied to what the question asks

diff.label: Alternatives
diff.good: One in the family, one from another

diff.label: Limit
diff.good: Stated, what results mean, partly reduced

exemplars.note: Both defenses are illustrative, and “Strong” rates method fit only. Either family could be defended well: the reasoning moves the level, not the family.
